1. Hepatotropic vs Non-hepatotropic Viruses and Outcomes of Infection

ScopeLimited to what her video covers. Her only red markings are the Rare entries in the outcomes table (section 7).
Hepatotropic virusesNon-hepatotropic viruses
TargetInfect hepatocytes directlyCause systemic infection with liver involvement
InjuryDirect cytotoxicity or immune-mediated killingIndirect: systemic spread, cytokines, immune-mediated injury, shock/hypoxia
ExamplesHepatitis A, B, C, D, E ("viral hepatitis")CMV, EBV, HSV, influenza (many others)
Hepatotropic vs non-hepatotropic viruses (slide 4) (click to enlarge)

Four outcomes of hepatitis infection

OutcomeFeatures
Acute hepatitisShort-term; symptomatic or asymptomatic; immune system clears virus → recovery. Viral titer peaks about when symptoms start; liver regenerates quickly.
Chronic hepatitisPersistent stable or fluctuating viral titers; symptoms vary and flare; persistent or intermittent liver injury. Repeated inflammation → repeated injury → fibrosis → cirrhosis → liver failure or HCC.
Carrier statePersistent stable or fluctuating viral titers, often asymptomatic, minimal to no liver injury; can still infect others; can reactivate. Often considered a version of chronic hepatitis.
Fulminant liver failureRare but severe: viral titer rises then falls rapidly as hepatocytes die (no hosts left) while symptoms and injury skyrocket from the immune response and toxicity; rapid liver failure.
Acute hepatitis: viral titer, symptoms, liver injury (slide 6) (click to enlarge)
Chronic hepatitis (slide 7) (click to enlarge)
Carrier state (slide 8) (click to enlarge)
Fulminant liver failure (slide 9) (click to enlarge)
  • Symptoms start around peak titer because most hepatotropic viruses cause little direct damage; symptoms appear when the immune response attacks infected hepatocytes.
  • Carrier vs chronic: both persistent, but chronic hepatitis has ongoing inflammation and damage; a carrier has little or none yet is still infectious.

2. Morphology: Acute vs Chronic Hepatitis

Acute hepatitisChronic hepatitis
Lobular inflammation across the parenchyma
Hepatocyte necrosis and apoptosis
Ballooning degeneration: enlarged hepatocytes with clear, fuzzy cytoplasm
Councilman body: highly eosinophilic apoptotic cell fragments
Cholestasis may occur (bile in canaliculi/hepatocytes)
Features depend on severity; steatosis in her image is likely a separate condition		Portal inflammation (dense infiltrate around portal tracts)
Interface hepatitis: inflammation spills into the parenchyma and damages hepatocytes at the portal-parenchymal border
Portal fibrosis or bridging fibrosis, which precedes cirrhosis
Acute hepatitis morphology (slide 10) (click to enlarge)
Chronic hepatitis morphology (slide 11) (click to enlarge)
Why fibrosis in chronic onlyChronic inflammation activates hepatic stellate cells to deposit collagen; duration is the major factor. Interface hepatitis is also prominent in chronic disease.

3. Enteric Hepatitis: HAV and HEV

Hepatitis A (HAV)

  • RNA virus, fecal-oral (contaminated food, water, seafood, close contact).
  • Acute hepatitis +/- symptoms (about 25% of all acute hepatitis); fulminant failure rare (0.1-0.3%), usually with underlying chronic liver disease; no chronic disease, no carrier state.
  • No direct cytotoxicity: damage is immune-mediated.
  • Timeline (graph): incubation 2-6 weeks (virus in feces), symptoms 2-12 weeks; IgM anti-HAV early, IgG anti-HAV later and persistent.
  • Nonspecific symptoms if any; self-limited (recovery within 3-6 months); HAV vaccine available.
Hepatitis A (slide 13) (click to enlarge)

Hepatitis E (HEV)

  • RNA virus, fecal-oral; acute hepatitis +/- symptoms.
  • Exception: fulminant failure is rare overall but 20% mortality in pregnant women.
  • No chronic or carrier state unless immunocompromised (HIV, organ transplant immunosuppression).
  • Zoonotic (monkeys, cats, pigs, dogs); epidemics in Asia, India, Africa, Mexico; US cases mostly after travel.
  • No direct cytotoxicity; immune-mediated. No HEV vaccine in the US.

HAVHEV
TransmissionFecal-oralFecal-oral

4. Hepatitis B (HBV)

  • DNA virus (the only DNA hepatitis virus); parenteral: blood and body fluids.
  • Outcomes: acute hepatitis (about 90%), chronic hepatitis, carrier state, rare fulminant failure. The primary infection associated with the term carrier state.
  • Transmission: sexual, contaminated needles, open wounds, perinatal (vertical); perinatal is about 90% of cases in high-incidence regions (Africa, Asia) and carries the highest risk of chronic infection. Adult infection is usually acute, often asymptomatic.
  • Both direct cytotoxicity and immune-mediated damage (unlike HAV).
  • Prevention: HBV vaccine.
Hepatitis B and its replication cycle (slide 14) (click to enlarge)
Replication (her brief walkthrough)Virion enters via the bile acid (NTCP) receptor → nucleus: viral DNA becomes cccDNA → transcribed to RNA → translated into virion components; reverse transcription of the RNA intermediate recreates the DNA in new virions → secreted. This repeats in a cell, amplifying the virus.

Complications and chronicity

  • Cirrhosis from repeated inflammation, repair and fibrosis → portal hypertension, HCC, liver failure.
  • Immune-complex deposition: glomerulonephritis, polyarteritis nodosa (vasculitis).
  • Why neonates? Immature immune response, less effective cytotoxic T-cell response against infected hepatocytes, so clearance is inefficient and infection is likely to become chronic.
  • Her slide outcome data: acute without symptoms 65% or with symptoms 25% with recovery; chronic 5-10% (most with perinatal transmission); fulminant failure 0.1-0.5%.

5. Hepatitis C (HCV)

  • RNA virus, parenteral (blood, rarely body fluids); slide lists sexual, contaminated needles, open wounds, perinatal.
  • Acute hepatitis, usually asymptomatic ("silent"); 80-90% progress to chronic hepatitis. Term "carrier state" is not used, but some chronic patients are asymptomatic and still infectious.
  • Why chronic: low-fidelity RNA polymerase makes errors → genetic variants → host antibodies no longer recognize them → persistence.
  • Replication: endocytosis → membrane fusion and uncoating → RNA released to cytoplasm for replication and translation → assembly in ER/Golgi → budding.
  • Risk of progression: older age, male, HBV or HIV co-infection, insulin resistance (diabetes, obesity), alcohol.
  • Complications: cirrhosis → HCC (one third of HCC cases in the US); mixed cryoglobulinemia.
  • No vaccine; targeted antivirals are standard of care.
Hepatitis C and replication (slide 21) (click to enlarge)
HCV acute vs chronic course (slide 22) (click to enlarge)
  • Acute: incubation 2-26 weeks before transaminases and HCV RNA rise, symptoms follow, then resolution. Chronic: HCV RNA and transaminases persist with symptom flares.

6. Hepatitis D (HDV)

  • RNA virus, parenteral, and occurs only with HBV infection.
  • Why: HDV is defective; it does not encode its own surface protein and needs HBsAg as its envelope to assemble and spread.
Hepatitis D (slide 23) (click to enlarge)
Co-infectionSuperinfection
DefinitionHDV acquired at the same time as HBVHDV acquired during chronic HBV infection
CourseTypically acute +/- symptoms with recovery; in IV drug users fulminant failure can occurIf HBV carrier: acute hepatitis with severe symptoms and recovery. Otherwise chronic HDV (80%); often becomes chronic if HBV is chronic
PrognosisLower risk of chronicityWorse: chronic disease and complications
  • In the US, most common among IV drug users.
  • Increases risk of cirrhosis and HCC versus HBV alone.
  • HBV vaccination is preventative (no separate HDV vaccine).

Final outcomes table (slide 30) (click to enlarge)
  • HAV: acute, self-limited, recovery in 3-6 months; fulminant 0.1-0.3%.
  • HBV: mostly acute; chronic less likely (5-10%) but common after perinatal transmission; "healthy carrier" state.
  • HCV: begins acute but most often becomes chronic (80-90%); *carrier state not used as a term. "Recognized" for acute-to-recovery would also be reasonable (her note).
  • HDV: coinfection acute with recovery (fulminant failure in IV drug users); superinfection severe acute in carriers, often chronic.
  • HEV: acute with recovery; chronic only in immunosuppressed; fulminant in pregnancy.

8. Study Guide Key: Guiding Questions

Her keyClick each question to reveal the answer from her key.
Why do symptoms start at peak viral titer rather than at acquisition?Most hepatotropic viruses cause little direct damage; symptoms arise when the immune response attacks infected hepatocytes, so they coincide with the peak immune response.
Chronic hepatitis vs carrier state?Both persistent infection. Chronic hepatitis has ongoing inflammation and damage; a carrier has neither but can still transmit.
A morphologic feature separating chronic from acute, and why?Portal or bridging fibrosis (chronic inflammation activates stellate cells to deposit collagen; duration is the major factor). Interface hepatitis is also prominent in chronic.
Sort the 5 viruses: route, nucleic acid, chronicity, HCC, vaccineEnteral: HAV, HEV. Parenteral: HBV, HCV, HDV. DNA: HBV; RNA: HAV, HCV, HDV, HEV. Chronic none/rare: HAV, HEV (rare exception in immunocompromised); possible: HBV, HDV; likely: HCV. HCC yes: HBV, HCV, HDV; no: HAV, HEV. Vaccine yes: HAV, HBV; no: HCV, HDV (HBV vaccine functionally protects), HEV.
Why are neonates at greater risk of chronic HBV?Immature immune response, less effective cytotoxic T-cell response against infected hepatocytes, inefficient clearance.
What features of HCV promote chronic infection?Error-prone RNA polymerase generates frequent mutations; antigenic variability lets it evade immune recognition and persist.
Why does HDV require HBV?HDV is defective and cannot make its own envelope; it needs HBV's HBsAg for assembly and transmission.
HDV co-infection vs superinfection?Co-infection: simultaneous with HBV; usually severe acute hepatitis with lower risk of chronicity. Superinfection: HDV in pre-existing chronic HBV; chronic disease, complications, worse prognosis.
Two exceptions in HEV course?(1) Pregnancy: increased fulminant failure and maternal mortality. (2) Immunocompromised: chronic infection with progressive liver disease.
